content: In statistics, the absolute deviation of an element within a data set is defined as the absolute difference between that specific element and a given reference point. Typically, this reference point is either the median or the mean of the data set. The average absolute deviation, also referred to as the average deviation, represents the mean (or expected value) of all absolute deviations within the data set. It serves as a summary statistic that quantifies the degree of statistical dispersion or variability in the data. The choice of the central tendency measure, such as the median or the mean, significantly influences the value of the average absolute deviation. For instance, in the data set {2, 2, 3, 4, 14}, the average absolute deviation calculated from the median is always less than or equal to the average absolute deviation calculated from the mean. In fact, the average absolute deviation from the median is always less than or equal to the average absolute deviation from any other fixed number. Furthermore, the average absolute deviation from the mean is always less than or equal to the standard deviation. This relationship can be demonstrated using Jensen's inequality. The mean absolute deviation specifically refers to the average absolute deviation calculated from the mean. It is a commonly used metric for assessing forecast errors in time series analysis. However, it is important to note that while the term mean deviation is often used interchangeably with mean absolute deviation, they are not technically the same. In its strict definition, the mean deviation (without applying the absolute value operation) of any data set from its mean is always zero. Lastly, the mean absolute deviation of a sample is considered a biased estimator of the mean absolute deviation of the entire population.
